what_it_does: Safety-critical embedded systems — think medical devices or industrial controllers — must sometimes prove to a remote auditor that their software actually ran the intended sequence of steps and was not tampered with. This is called control flow attestation: you record the path a program took through its own code and send that record to a verifier. Doing so usually requires inserting extra instructions into the program (instrumentation) and frequently pausing the main code to capture and transmit the trace, both of which slow the device down. RAP-Track instead piggybacks on two hardware features already present in many low-cost microcontrollers: a Micro Trace Buffer (a small on-chip buffer that silently records branch events as the processor runs) and a Data Watchpoint and Trace Unit (a hardware monitor that triggers on specific memory accesses). By letting these existing hardware units capture the control flow record in parallel with normal execution — without touching the program itself — the paper claims it avoids instrumentation overhead and the costly context switches that plagued earlier approaches.
